title: Wash your bowl
hook: a new monk asks for teaching, Zhaozhou asks if he's eaten, and says: then wash your bowl (Gateless Gate, case 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ryokan gave a thief his robe and wished he could give him the moon. Your line was the moon stays. What did you give away freely? Day forty-seven.

You've finally done it. You signed up for the class, joined the gym, opened the book everyone talks about. And on the first day you walk in ready for the big secret. Tell me the thing. The real thing. The key. Now picture a young monk in China, more than a thousand years ago, doing exactly that. He's just entered the monastery. He finds the old master, Zhaozhou, one of the most famous teachers in the history of Zen, and he asks, earnestly: I've just arrived. Please, teach me. And Zhaozhou asks him about breakfast. Today's story is wash your bowl.
screen: `TELL ME THE REAL THING.` → `A NEW MONK ARRIVES.` → `PLEASE, TEACH ME.`

segments.voice: This one comes from a real book: the Gateless Gate, a collection of forty-eight short Zen cases gathered in China in the twelve hundreds by a monk named Wumen. It's case seven, and it's only a few lines long. The monk says: I've just entered the monastery. Please teach me. Zhaozhou asks: have you eaten your rice porridge? The monk says: yes, I have. And Zhaozhou says: then wash your bowl. The book says the monk understood. That's it. No lecture. No secret. The monk wanted something special, and Zhaozhou pointed him at the dishes. Here's what makes it more than a brush-off. In a Zen monastery, washing your bowl isn't a chore you do before the practice starts. It is the practice. Eat when you eat. Wash when you wash. Do the next plain thing completely, with your whole attention, instead of reaching past it for something grander. The teaching isn't hidden somewhere else. It's in your hands, in the warm water, in the bowl. Zen kept saying this, in many voices. The Japanese teacher Dogen, who studied in China and came home in 1227, wrote a whole set of instructions for the monastery cook, and treated washing rice and scrubbing pots as seriously as sitting in the meditation hall. And notice what Zhaozhou didn't say. He didn't call the porridge unimportant, or tell the monk to hurry past breakfast to reach the real teaching. He sent him back to the bowl he'd just used. You don't need a mountain or a retreat. You have a sink, and one dish. That's enough.
screen: `THE GATELESS GATE, CASE SEVEN.` · `HAVE YOU EATEN YOUR PORRIDGE?` · `THE DISHES ARE THE PRACTICE.` · `DOGEN'S INSTRUCTIONS FOR THE COOK.` · then, large: `THEN WASH YOUR BOWL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash one dish with full attention. If you can, go to a sink now. If not, picture it clearly. Feel the temperature of the water. Feel the weight of the dish. Watch the soap, the way it slides. Wash it slowly, front and back, as if it were the only thing to do today. When your mind runs ahead, and it will, come back to the bowl. Dry it. Put it away. The bell holds the time.
Zhaozhou. The Zen master who answered a monk's plea for teaching by sending him to wash his breakfast bowl.
Your line: eat when you eat. Today, when you catch yourself waiting for the real thing to start, do the next small task with your whole attention. Day forty-seven.

screen: `DAY 47 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FINGER AND THE MOON.`

howItsDone: In Zen monasteries, meals are eaten in silence from a set of nested bowls that each monk cleans at the table, and daily work like cooking and cleaning is treated as part of practice, not a break from it.

original.note: Chinese: go wash your bowl, Zhaozhou's words in case seven of the Gateless Gate.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old monk dodging a question.
what it means: the practice isn't somewhere else; it's the plain task in your hands, done completely.
what a scholar hears: Wumenguan, the Gateless Gate, case seven; Zhaozhou Congshen, a Tang-dynasty master, whom tradition says lived to about 120.

notes: Gateless Gate: 48 cases, compiled by Wumen Huikai, published 1228 ('in the twelve hundreds'). Case 7 paraphrased; English translations in circulation (Senzaki 1934, etc.) are not quoted.
Chinese 洗鉢盂去 (xǐ bōyú qù) as Zhaozhou's words: confirm text and the simplified pronunciation.
Zhaozhou Congshen (778–897) 'lived to about 120' is traditional; given as tradition.

Audit (second sample): the teach's Brother Lawrence 'pots and pans' passage was cut because day 87 tells his whole story (and day 87's practice echoed this one); it is replaced with Dogen's Instructions for the Cook (Tenzo Kyokun, 1237; Dogen returned from China in 1227), and the stock line 'this is good news' is gone. Match pair, screen head and source updated. Confirm the Dogen dates and that the Tenzo Kyokun treats washing rice and pots as practice.
